mcqs.question: Why does matching riders to drivers need a spatial index instead of scanning every driver's stored location?
options: Driver locations change too fast to store in a database at all
Scanning every driver on every match request turns a lookup into an O(n) scan, and that cost compounds as the fleet grows
Riders and drivers cannot use the same location data structure
GPS coordinates are too imprecise to index
mcqs.explanation: The scaling problem is the point: an O(n) scan per match request gets slower as the fleet grows, which is exactly backwards. Locations are stored fine in a database, index structures can serve both riders and drivers, and GPS precision isn't the issue here.

mcqs.question: When does batched assignment (collecting requests over a short window and solving jointly) beat greedy nearest-driver matching?
options: Always — batching is strictly better and should be the default everywhere
Never — greedy matching is always optimal for total pickup distance
In dense areas at peak demand, where joint optimization measurably cuts total pickup distance across many simultaneous requests
Only when there is exactly one driver available in the entire city
mcqs.explanation: Batching pays off when there's enough simultaneous demand and supply to actually improve on a joint solve — dense, peak-time areas. It adds latency, so it's not a universal default, greedy isn't always optimal, and a single-driver scenario has nothing to batch.

mcqs.question: Two riders' match requests both resolve to the same nearest driver at nearly the same instant. What prevents both from claiming that driver?
options: Nothing extra is needed — findNearestDriver already prevents this by design
The mobile app retries automatically until only one request remains
Drivers are duplicated per request so each rider effectively gets their own copy
An atomic conditional update that claims the driver only if still available; whichever update actually changes a row wins, and the loser re-matches
mcqs.explanation: findNearestDriver only reads, so it can't prevent a double-claim on its own — the claim itself must be an atomic conditional write. Retries and duplicating drivers don't address the underlying race.

mcqs.question: What goes wrong if every driver location ping triggers a full re-scan or re-sort of all drivers?
options: The system's cost scales with driver count times ping frequency, getting slower as exactly the fleet you're trying to serve grows
Nothing — pings are infrequent enough that this is always fine
It only affects drivers, never riders, so it's an acceptable trade-off
It causes GPS coordinates to become inaccurate over time
mcqs.explanation: Pings are frequent and continuous, so an O(n) response to each one scales badly with fleet size — the opposite of what you want. It does affect match latency for riders too, and GPS accuracy is unrelated.
